subject: retail-barring-orders-bill-2025
note: Four forks over the as-introduced print. None is materialised: every one was resolved at encode time or delegated to a fact the court supplies, which is the same result the BNA smoke run and the Jersey charities cleanroom reached over their own texts, and it is a real finding rather than an empty register. Completeness is NOT claimed and cannot be: no procedure establishes that every ambiguity was found, which is why SPEC.md makes it HG1's judgement and not a checker's. Two of the four (F-3, F-4) are the interpretive questions underneath incidents B-02 and B-01; recording them here is what keeps the difference visible between 'the Bill is ambiguous' and 'the Bill has a gap', which are different findings with different repairs.

source.quote: A person who procures another person to commit retail violence is taken to have also committed the retail violence.

readings.description: The deeming in s 6(2) is unqualified: it attaches to the act of procuring and says nothing about where the procurer was. A person who procures retail violence from outside the premises, or from another State, is taken to have committed it. Encoded as an independent disjunct beside s 6(1), so the procurer's own presence is never tested.

citations.cite: Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 6(2) — the subsection carries no locational words, in contrast with s 6(1), which opens 'while on retail premises'
Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 4(a), (e)-(f) — objects of protecting persons on retail premises and holding those who commit retail violence accountable

readings.description: s 6(2) deems the procurer to have committed 'the retail violence', and 'retail violence' is what s 6(1) defines, which includes being on retail premises. On this reading the deeming imports the whole of s 6(1), presence included, so an absent procurer is outside the section.
readings.rejection_rationale: It empties the subsection. A procurer who is on the premises and engages in the behaviour is already caught by s 6(1) directly, and a procurer who is on the premises but does nothing else is not 'engaging in' any of the s 6(1)(a)-(e) behaviours in their own person. Reading the presence requirement into s 6(2) would leave it with almost no work to do, which is not a reading to prefer over one that gives it obvious work.

taken.rationale: The unqualified reading is the natural one and is the only one on which s 6(2) adds anything to s 6(1).

witnesses: `the actor commits retail violence` — an incident with `the actor is on the premises` FALSE and `the actor procured another to commit it` TRUE is TRUE on the reading taken and FALSE on the rejected one

entries.delegated_field: the respondent has reached 10 years of age

site.anchor: the court may make an RBO

source.quote: (b) the person is an individual who has reached 10 years of age.

readings.description: The age is tested when the court makes the order. s 10 opens 'A court may make an RBO against a person if', and every other limb of s 10 is a condition on the making; (b) reads as one more of them.

citations.cite: Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 10, chapeau — 'A court may make an RBO against a person if'

Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) ss 21(2), 40(2), 48(1) — the Bill's other age tests are all pinned to a named moment, and s 10(b) is the one that is not, which is why the chapeau has to supply it

readings.description: The age is tested when the retail violence was committed, so a person who was 9 at the time of the incident and 10 by the hearing could not be made subject to an RBO.
readings.foreclosure: Not foreclosed by the words, and s 8(2) leaves up to twelve months between the conduct and the application in which a child can cross the boundary. It is non-operative in the encoding because the chapeau ties every other limb of s 10 to the moment of making and nothing in (b) displaces that. It is recorded as arguable rather than rejected because the contrary reading is one a respondent could run, and because the age of criminal responsibility it echoes is measured at the time of the conduct.

citations.cite: The Criminal Code (WA) s 29 — criminal responsibility is measured at the time of the act, which is the source of the 10-year figure and the reason a reader may expect the same measuring point
Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 8(2) — an application may be made up to twelve months after the conduct, so the two moments can fall on opposite sides of a birthday

taken.rationale: Delegated rather than computed: the encoding takes `the respondent has reached 10 years of age` as a fact the court supplies, so the reading does not have to be settled in order to run the rule. A court applying the other reading supplies a different value for the same field and the encoding still answers.

site.anchor: section 63(2) obliges the server to ask the firearms questions

source.quote: A police officer who serves a firearms RBO personally or effects substituted service of a firearms RBO under section 56(3) or 57(5) orally must --

readings.description: The subsection means what it says: the duty falls on a police officer, and reaches substituted service only where effected orally. Six of the nine service routes the Bill permits therefore carry no firearms inquiry at all.

citations.cite: Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 63(2) — 'A police officer who', and 'orally' qualifying the substituted-service limb
Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 63(4) — the Commissioner's duty arises 'on receipt of the police copy', which presupposes a police officer completed one under s 63(2)(b)

Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 55(2)(a), (b), (d), (e) — personal service may be effected by a registrar, an authorised person, a custodial officer or a prison officer, none of whom s 63(2) reaches

readings.description: Read purposively against the object of the section, the duty attaches to the service of a firearms RBO however effected, and 'police officer' and 'orally' describe the expected case rather than limit the duty.
readings.foreclosure: Non-operative because the machinery s 63 builds is police machinery throughout: the questions are recorded on 'the police copy' (s 63(2)(b)) and the Commissioner's duty is triggered by receipt of that copy (s 63(4)). A registrar or prison officer has no police copy to complete, so the purposive reading cannot be given effect without also reading a police copy into their hands, which is more than construction will bear.

citations.cite: Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 4(a), (d) — objects of protecting persons on retail premises and public confidence, which the firearms notification serves
Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 63(5), (6) — the offences the notification enables, which on the narrow reading are unavailable in six of nine service routes

taken.rationale: Encoded on the narrow reading because that is what the text says and because the wider reading cannot be implemented without inventing a police copy for a non-police server. The consequence of the narrow reading is incident B-02: recording the fork here keeps separate the question whether the Bill is AMBIGUOUS (it is, mildly) from the finding that on its natural reading it has a COVERAGE GAP (it does).

witnesses: `the Commissioner must notify under section 63(4)` over `personal service by a prison officer` — FALSE on the reading taken, TRUE on the arguable reading (rbo-cases.l4, `B-02 scenario A -- prison officer serves personally`)

`the Commissioner must notify under section 63(4)` over `substituted service effected by post` — FALSE on the reading taken, TRUE on the arguable reading (rbo-cases.l4, `B-02 scenario B -- substituted service by post`)

site.anchor: the orders the court may make under section 39

source.quote: At a hearing fixed under section 38(1)(a) the court may make an order cancelling the RBO.

readings.description: s 39 states the orders available at each kind of hearing and states different sets for each, so the enumeration is exhaustive. At a s 38(1)(a) hearing the court may cancel and nothing else, and an application it declines to grant has no order by which it can be disposed of. Encoded as two lists, with the outcome `no order is available under section 39` naming the resulting state.

citations.cite: Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 39(1) — the parallel subsection expressly confers a dismissal power, so its absence from s 39(2) is a difference the drafter made

Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 41(1) — supplies a dismissal power for a hearing fixed under s 37 'or 38(1)(a)', but only on non-attendance, which shows the drafter had s 38 dismissal in contemplation and provided for one case only

readings.description: s 45 applies the practice and procedure of the Magistrates Court (Civil Proceedings) Act 2004, which supplies a general power to dispose of an application, so the court may dismiss at a s 38 hearing notwithstanding s 39(2)'s silence.
readings.foreclosure: Non-operative in the encoding because s 45 applies 'unless otherwise provided by this Act', and s 39 does otherwise provide: it enumerates the orders available at each hearing, differently for each. An enumeration that varies by hearing type is hard to read as leaving a general power intact. It is recorded as arguable rather than rejected because a court faced with an undisposable application would very likely reach for exactly this argument, and because the alternative is an application that can never be determined.

citations.cite: Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 45 — practice and procedure of the Magistrates Court (Civil Proceedings) Act 2004 applies unless otherwise provided
Retail Barring Orders Bill 2025 (WA) s 35(2)(a) — 'or the application to vary is otherwise determined' shows the drafter contemplated determinations outside the named orders

taken.rationale: Encoded on the exhaustive reading because that is what the two subsections say when read against each other, and because encoding the arguable reading would paper over the defect the section has. Incident B-01 is the consequence. If the arguable reading is right the defect is cured by general law rather than absent, which is a weaker answer than a drafting fix and is why the incident stands either way.

witnesses: `the outcome under section 39` over `section 38(1)(a) -- a cancellation heard in the absence of the person bound` with the court not satisfied — `no order is available under section 39` on the reading taken, `the application is dismissed` on the arguable reading (rbo-cases.l4, § B-01)
